newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse chief seeks jobs market reforms.
newsitem.headline: German bourse chief seeks jobs market reforms.

text.p: Thorough labour market deregulation is needed if Germany is to hold its own as a key European financial centre, bourse chief executive Werner Seifert said on Monday.

Addressing the parliamentary group of Germany's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), Seifert said the nation's tradionally tight job market restrictions inhibited employment and jarred with a market economy.
"Politicians should withdraw from labour market regulation," he said. "They should remove those restrictions which inhibit the development of wage levels directed by a market economy."

Among other changes, Seifert urged the wider adoption of performance-related pay models such as those which pay managers partly in stock options. Current pay structures were geared toward achieving stability, not performance, he said.

Labour market reform was just as important for financial markets as the broad reforms of securities laws and company regulations which have been implemented or developed in Germany in the past few years, Seifert said.

"It is not enough for politicians to try to promote capital market efficiency. This must be combined with a reorganisation of the jobs market to allow more entrepreneurship and thus reduce unemployment," he added.

Seifert also bemoaned the lack of talented personnel in German financial institutions and said more legislative measures were needed -- such as cutting the top level of income tax -- to persude market stars to move to Frankfurt.
"As long as a good London trader views a transfer to Frankfurt as a punishment, we have a disadvantage as a location," Seifert said.
Nonetheless Seifert said Frankfurt had every chance of holding its own against Paris and London as a major financial centre in the future.

He said the current overhaul of the overburdened pensions system would inevitably spark an explosion of interest in investment alternatives, helping to break Germans' legendary attachment to their regular savings accounts.
Moreover the launch of the Euro, as planned for January 1 1999, would create an enormous opportunity for Frankfurt, although not its only one.
"There is every reason for confidence," Seifert said.
